title: The Orphan Years
year: 571 CE — 579 CE, from infancy to his eighth year
teaser: Four households before he was nine — a desert nurse, his mother, his grandfather, then an uncle for forty years.

layers.title: The Desert of Banu Sa'd
layers.subtitle: The tents where a Makkan infant was raised
layers.content:
Banu Sa'd bin Bakr grazed their flocks in the dry high country away from Makkah, in the direction of Ta'if. It was thin land in any year. In the season the infant was carried out to them it was thinner still — the sirah records a year of drought and famine, wells low, she-camels giving nothing.

Town families in Makkah sent their infants to such places deliberately. The reason the sources give is practical: the open country built strong bodies, and it gave a child the pure speech and manners of the Bedouin. A boy came back with the desert in his lungs and its Arabic in his mouth.

The household he entered had names. Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb nursed him. Her husband was Al-Harith bin Abd al-Uzza, called Abu Kabshah, of the same tribe. There were foster brothers and sisters: Abdullah bin Al-Harith, Anisah bint Al-Harith, and a girl recorded as Hudhafah or Judhamah but known to everyone as Ash-Shayma'. She is the one the reports single out — the one who carried him about and took care of him.

He was not the only child of Abd al-Muttalib's line fed by those women. His uncle Hamzah was suckled by the same two nurses who suckled him, Thuwaybah and As-Sa'diyyah, which made an uncle also a milk-brother.

Two years passed and he was weaned. Halimah took him back to Makkah and asked to keep him longer, pressing the request. She was granted it. The tents of Banu Sa'd held him again, and kept him until he was four or five years old.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham 1/162-164

layers.title: The Road to Al-Abwa
layers.subtitle: Five hundred kilometres, and a grave beside it
layers.content:
He came back to his mother at about five. Aminah had him for a little over a year.

Then, in his sixth year, she went north. Her purpose was the grave of her husband Abdullah at Yathrib. The distance is roughly five hundred kilometres of caravan road, covered at the pace of a loaded camel, and she took the boy, his grandfather Abd al-Muttalib, and a servant woman, Umm Ayman. They stayed a month. On the way home Aminah fell severely ill and died at Al-Abwa.

Al-Abwa is not a place remembered for itself. It lies near Waddan, which the sirah places about twenty-nine miles out from Madinah, on the strip of road every Makkan caravan used. She was buried there. Her son continued to Makkah with his grandfather.

He would come back to that ground. In Safar of the second year after the migration, at the head of seventy men, the Prophet ﷺ led his first expedition in person, and its destination was Al-Abwa and Waddan. He reached Waddan without incident, made a non-aggression pact with Amr bin Makhshi Ad-Damri, and returned after fifteen days. The reports say nothing about the grave. They do not say he stopped at it, and no one should claim he did.

So the account stands at two losses before his seventh year: a father he never saw, and a mother who died on the road home from visiting that father's grave.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham 1/168, and Al-Mawahibul-Ladunniyah 1/75 for the expedition to Al-Abwa

layers.title: The Third Guardian
layers.subtitle: A grandfather dies and a brother steps in
layers.content:
Abd al-Muttalib was an old man with a large family. The sources list ten sons, some say eleven, some thirteen, and six daughters. Into that crowded house came a grandson with no father and now no mother, and the old man preferred him openly to his own children.

He kept him close. When the year was rainless and the Quraysh came asking him to pray for water, one report — from Ibn Asakir on the authority of Jalhamah bin Arfutah, and it should be given as a report and not more — describes Abd al-Muttalib walking to the Ka'bah with a boy beside him and praying there for rain, and the rain coming.

Then the third bereavement. When the Prophet ﷺ was eight years, two months and ten days old, Abd al-Muttalib died at Makkah. In eight years he had lost a father, a mother and a grandfather.

The charge passed to Abu Talib. This mattered more than the sirah pauses to explain. Abd al-Muttalib had many sons, and Abu Talib was not the eldest. He was the full brother of Abdullah — same father, same mother — and by the reckoning of Arab kinship the boy was his in a way he was not any other uncle's.

Abu Talib took it on completely. He placed the boy among his own children and preferred him to them. He singled him out with respect, held him in high esteem, and did so for forty years. From then on, how a man treated this nephew determined how Abu Talib treated that man.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham 1/108-109 and 1/168, and Mukhtasar Seeratir-Rasul by Sheikh Abdullah An-Najdi pp. 15-16

layers.title: The Shepherd's Wage
layers.subtitle: The work Allah gave every prophet before the message
layers.content:
No revelation was sent down about these years. That should be said plainly. The Qur'an does not narrate the death of Aminah or the death of Abd al-Muttalib. What it does is carry the fact of the orphaning forward into law, addressing the man who had been that child: «فَأَمَّا الْيَتِيمَ فَلَا تَقْهَرْ» — 'So as for the orphan, do not oppress him.' (93:9) The command to protect orphans was given to one.

What the years themselves record is work. He had no fixed trade in early youth. He herded sheep for Banu Sa'd, and he herded them in Makkah for a wage.

This is not an incidental detail, because he later described it as the pattern. The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah sent no prophet who was not a shepherd of sheep. The Companions asked whether this included him. He said yes — he used to graze them for the people of Makkah for a few qararit, small coins.

Consider what the work is. A flock cannot be driven by force; it has to be led, and led at its own speed. It must be counted, and the count kept. Water and grazing have to be found before the animals need them. The weak and the young set the pace. The days are long, silent, and spent outdoors under an open sky with nothing to do but watch and think.

He was learning a trade. He was also being given, years before he knew it, the exact habits of the work he would be handed at forty.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 93:9 — 'So as for the orphan, do not oppress him'
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Al-Bukhari, Book of Hiring — narrated by Abu Hurairah, that Allah sent no prophet who did not herd sheep
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Darussalam — citing Ibn Hisham 1/166 and Sahih Al-Bukhari

layers.title: What It Left Behind
layers.subtitle: The debt that came back forty years later
layers.content:
Four households held him before he was nine, and none of them was owed him. Halimah took an orphan when no reward could be expected from him. Abd al-Muttalib set him above his own sons. Abu Talib, one uncle among several, took the responsibility and carried it for four decades. Nothing in that chain was obligation. All of it was kindness given to a child who could not repay it.

He repaid it anyway, and the sirah keeps the receipt. In the eighth year after the migration, after the fighting at Hunayn, the captives of Hawazin were brought in. Among them was a woman who gave her name as Ash-Shayma' bint Al-Harith As-Sa'diyyah — the foster sister who had carried him in the desert of Banu Sa'd, now a prisoner of the man she had minded. He recognised her by a mark. He honoured her, spread his own garment on the ground and seated her on it, released her, and sent her back to her people.

He was by then the most powerful man in Arabia. She was a captive from a defeated tribe. Fifty years had passed, and he still owed her, and he paid.

The thing to carry out of these years is small and difficult. He did not treat his losses as a licence. Fatherless, motherless, passed from house to house — he grew up owing gratitude rather than collecting grievances, and he was still settling those accounts when he had the power to ignore them entirely.
layers.source: Safiur-Rahman Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, Darussalam — account of Ash-Shayma' among the captives of Hunayn

quiz.prompt: Which tribe were Halimah and her household from?

options.text: Banu Sa'd bin Bakr
Banu Kinanah
Thaqif of Ta'if
Banu An-Najjar of Yathrib

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — citing Ibn Hisham 1/162-164
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her husband was Al-Harith bin Abd al-Uzza, called Abu Kabshah, of the same tribe. Decades later, when Hawazin was defeated at Hunayn, Banu Sa'd bin Bakr were among the captives brought before him.

options.text: A second wet nurse who suckled him after Halimah
His foster sister, daughter of Al-Harith, who took care of him in the desert
The servant woman who travelled with Aminah to Yathrib
A daughter of Abd al-Muttalib who raised him after Aminah died

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — citing Ibn Hisham 1/162-164
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her given name is recorded as Hudhafah or Judhamah; Ash-Shayma' is what she was called. She appears once in childhood and once again as a captive at Hunayn, roughly fifty years apart.

quiz.prompt: Where did Aminah die, and on what journey?

options.text: In Makkah, shortly after her son was returned to her by Halimah
At Ta'if, on a trading journey with Abd al-Muttalib
At Al-Abwa, returning from visiting her husband's grave at Yathrib
At Yathrib itself, and she was buried beside Abdullah

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — citing Ibn Hisham 1/168
quiz.scholar_reflection: She set out on a road of roughly five hundred kilometres to visit a grave, stayed a month, and died on the way home. Al-Abwa lies near Waddan, on the caravan road between Makkah and Madinah.

quiz.prompt: Why did guardianship pass specifically to Abu Talib, when Abd al-Muttalib had many sons?

options.text: He was the eldest of Abd al-Muttalib's sons
He was the wealthiest and best able to afford another child
He was the full brother of Abdullah — the same father and the same mother
He was chosen by lot among the brothers at the Ka'bah

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — citing Ibn Hisham 1/108-109, 1/168
quiz.scholar_reflection: Abd al-Muttalib is recorded as having ten sons, with some reports naming eleven or thirteen. Abu Talib was not the eldest. Full brotherhood with Abdullah is what placed the child in his house, and he kept him there for forty years.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say about prophets and the herding of sheep?

options.text: That shepherding is the most honourable of trades and better than commerce
That Allah sent no prophet who was not a shepherd of sheep — including himself, for a few qararit
That he herded sheep only in the desert of Banu Sa'd and never in Makkah
That prophets were forbidden to take wages for any work

quiz.citation: Sahih Al-Bukhari, Book of Hiring — narrated by Abu Hurairah
quiz.scholar_reflection: Qararit were small coins. He named the wage. A prophet's account of his own working life included the rate of pay, which tells you something about how the sirah handles his humanity.

quiz.prompt: The Qur'an does not narrate the death of his mother or his grandfather. It takes the fact of his orphaning and turns it into a command: do not oppress the orphan. What do you make of that use of his life?
quiz.slider_label: How much of your own hardship do you think is meant for others?

options.text: His pain was made into a law that protects other people — that is what it was for
Allah does not narrate the wound; He legislates from it, and that restraint is itself instructive
The command lands harder coming from someone who had been on the receiving end
I am not sure a person's suffering has a purpose beyond itself, and I sit with that

quiz.citation: Quran 93:9 — 'So as for the orphan, do not oppress him'
quiz.scholar_reflection: The verse is an imperative, not a consolation. Allah addressed the grown man about a category he had belonged to, and the address was a duty rather than a comfort.

quiz.prompt: For years his work was to lead a flock — at its speed, counting it, finding water before it was needed, letting the weakest set the pace. How much of that do you think transferred to leading people?
quiz.slider_label: How much do you believe ordinary work forms character?

options.text: Almost all of it — the habits are the same and he practised them for years
Some of it, but the parallel can be pushed too far and turned into a neat lesson
The real training was the solitude, not the sheep
It mattered mainly as honest labour — that he worked at all, for a small wage

quiz.citation: Sahih Al-Bukhari, Book of Hiring — narrated by Abu Hurairah
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not present shepherding as a metaphor. He presented it as a fact about every prophet before him. The pattern was Allah's, and it was consistent enough that he pointed it out.

quiz.prompt: Abd al-Muttalib had ten sons of his own and openly preferred his orphaned grandson to all of them. What do you think that did to a boy — and to the household?
quiz.slider_label: How do you weigh being favoured against being resented?

options.text: It gave him a security that his losses had otherwise stripped away
It must have cost him something with his uncles, who saw a nephew placed above them
An old man's favour is fragile — it lasted two years and then he was orphaned again
It taught him early that standing comes from someone choosing you, not from what you own

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — citing Ibn Hisham 1/168
quiz.scholar_reflection: The uncles tried to move him off the mattress and were told to leave him. Whatever the old man saw, his sons did not see it, and one of those sons was Abu Lahab.

quiz.prompt: At Hunayn he was the most powerful man in Arabia. Ash-Shayma' was a captive from a defeated tribe. He spread his own garment for her and released her. What is the weight of that scene for you?
quiz.slider_label: How long do you carry a debt of kindness?

options.text: Power did not cancel the debt — fifty years later it was still owed and still paid
He honoured the woman who cared for him when he was worth nothing to anyone
It shows he never rewrote his own history to start at his success
Spreading his garment on the ground was the point — the gesture cost him status deliberately

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Ash-Shayma' among the captives of Hunayn
quiz.scholar_reflection: She had to introduce herself. He recognised her by a mark. Then he did more than release her — he seated her on his own garment, in front of an army, and sent her home.

quiz.prompt: Halimah, Aminah, Abd al-Muttalib, Abu Talib — none of them owed him anything, and each gave. What does a childhood built entirely on other people's kindness produce in a person?
quiz.slider_label: How aware are you of what was given to you unearned?

options.text: Gratitude, because he could see plainly that he had not built any of it himself
A sense of obligation to others that outlasted every one of them
It could equally have produced resentment — that it did not is the remarkable part
An understanding that provision comes from Allah through people, not from people

quiz.citation: Al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — the years of the Prophet's guardianship
quiz.scholar_reflection: Four guardians in eight years, and not one of them was required to take him. He spent his life repaying people who had not asked to be repaid, which is a harder discipline than paying a debt you agreed to.
